articles.title: Unidentified Murder review – playful sendup of alien abduction and true crime influencers in Hong Kong
articles.summary: Childhood friends claim to have witnessed the disappearance of a schoolkid in this low-budget comedy caper that pushes limits of storytelling. Modestly scaled and intricately structured, Kwok Ka-Hei and Jack Lee Chun-Kit’s comedy is a capriciously playful send-up of true crime aficionados and…
body: The film unfolds in a series of increasingly tricksy complications and reversals. All of a sudden, apparent victims are revealed to be scheming masterminds, and vice versa. As most of the actions take place in the forest where the abduction supposedly occurred, the plot derives comic relief from the increasingly blurred line between truth and playacting. Largely shot with handheld cameras, it has a visual style that lends authenticity to representations of online media, though occasionally this distracts from the physical comedy performed by the cast. The constant twists also turn into bit of a competitive sport, meaning the film becomes more of a writing exercise than anything else.

At the same time, considering the modest budget, the film-makers’ efforts at pushing the limits of meta storytelling are quite admirable. But what keeps Unidentified Murder engaging is the chemistry between Ling Man-lung and Ronald Lam, who compellingly capture a sense of genuine friendship amid a vortex of chaotic mishaps and shenanigans.

articles.title: ‘Sharks are my film stars’: how the Jacques Cousteau of the North Sea finally unlocked its beauty
articles.summary: Epic plankton blooms make filming in the North Sea notoriously difficult. But a new documentary gives a rare glimpse of the kaleidoscopic life – seals, sharks, tuna, orcas and shorthorn sculpins – lurking beneath its waves.
body: The North Sea, as even its greatest admirers will concede, often glowers an unappetising grey or brown. And we assume that its dull exterior is matched by sediment-filled waters where little life dwells. For years, the friends and family of Peter van Rodijnen wondered why the Dutch cinematographer and diving fanatic spent so much time exploring “this murky bowl of soup”. But, inspired by a childhood of watching Jacques Cousteau’s adventures in rather more enticingly temperate waters, Van Rodijnen’s dedication to North Sea diving gradually revealed its hidden wonders.

Over 20 years, as camera technology improved, Van Rodijnen obtained more and more amazing footage of marine life near his home on the Netherlands coast. Nearly a decade ago, he teamed up with director Mark Verkerk. “We started with the idea,” says Van Rodijnen, “that if somebody can make a movie about the North Sea, it’s got to be us.”

articles.title: France’s Halley Production Boards Thriller ‘Carro Seco,’ About Killer Who Targets Unscrupulous Barcelona Real Estate Speculators (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.summary: Paris-based Halley Production has boarded Javier Polo’s feature film thriller project “Carro Seco” (“Carreau”), showcased at the upcoming Iberseries & Platino Industria’s Co-Production and Financing Forum in Madrid.
body: Dressed like a vintage pétanque player, the vigilante is driven by the social impact of gentrification. Casting himself as a housing Robin Hood, he justifies his crimes as acts committed for the common good.
As two detectives navigate the investigation, public opinion splits between viewing the murderer as a heroic housing vigilante or a psychopath.

“‘Carro Seco’ uses the tension of a psychological thriller to address one of today’s most urgent social conflicts: silent evictions and real estate speculation,” says Polo. “What sets it apart is the contrast between that social nightmare and a unique, ritualistic iconography; turning an innocent neighborhood sport like pétanque into a deadly weapon accompanied by French chanson. It is a film that challenges the viewer with an uncomfortable moral dilemma about justice, boundaries, and empathy.”

Halley Production’s international co-productions include such cross-border hits as Javier Fesser’s 2018 crowd-pleaser “Champions,” Manuel Gómez Pereira’s 2025 Goya-winning Spanish hit “ The Dinner ” and the forthcoming drama “ Primo Viaggio.”

articles.title: ‘Strawberry and Chocolate’ Star Jorge Perugorría and Brazil’s Thiago Lacerda Lead Havana-Set ‘Hotel Nacional’ (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.summary: Cuba’s Jorge Perugorría, best known for his lead role in the iconic Oscar-nominated Cuban classic “Strawberry and Chocolate” (“Fresa y Chocolate”), has been cast in the upcoming film, “Hotel Nacional” which participates in the Iberseries & Platino Industria Co-Production and Financing Forum.
body: As Bruno and Pilar grow closer, they wander the streets of Havana and the corridors of the hotel they share, drinking, talking, and confronting the ghosts that haunt them—through alcohol, guilt, and each other.
It will be helmed by writer, director and producer Diego Corsini (“Adiós Madrid”) in his eighth feature film outing as a director.

“Rubén is a 60-year-old Cuban who has lived his entire life in Havana and has spent more than 30 years as the bartender at the Hotel Nacional’s bar. With his family scattered since his children moved abroad, his work is the only thing that distracts him from his loneliness, ever since his wife passed away a few years ago,” Corsini explained.

He added: “At the bar, he has his ‘occasional friends’—the tourists staying at the hotel, with whom he often manages to have deep conversations, frequently becoming a confidant. The arrival of Bruno and Pilar will leave a lasting mark on him, not only because of the bond they will gradually develop, but also because of the Brazilian’s story, which ultimately contains a hidden element that will be revealed toward the end of the film.”

articles.title: ‘You Can See Everything’ Review: Nathan Fielder’s Documentary About Elizabeth Holmes Is a Shameless, Fascinating, Reality-TV-Eats-Its-Tale Look at Entitled Duplicity
articles.summary: "You Can See Everything" is about the furthest thing from a "pure" documentary you’ve ever seen. That’s part of its appeal — it’s a one-a-kind reality-TV-as-hangout-movie psychodrama circus.
body: It's a hangout-movie portrait of the Theranos fraudster, which is really Fielder's way of asking: What makes someone like Elizabeth Holmes tick?

Fielder isn’t here to throw open the question of Elizabeth Holmes’ guilt. He wants to know what made her tick. But why, you may ask, is the comedian behind shows like “The Curse” and “The Rehearsal” making a three-hour movie about the woman who became America’s youngest self-made female billionaire by convincing the world that she’d created a revolutionary new means of blood testing? Holmes, after her conviction, stayed out of the public eye, but shortly before her prison sentence was set to begin she decided she wanted someone to document her last days of freedom. Maybe she wanted to have her say?

The Elizabeth Holmes we see has a winsome soft presence, with a Cupid’s-bow grin and eyes that beam without blinking too much. She resembles the ’80s and ’90s actress Kim Greist, and has a manner that’s disarming in its gentleness. Yet when Fielder asks about the crimes she was convicted of, she pleads a strange kind of ignorance. She claims she did nothing wrong, and it’s clear she believes it. But how is that possible?

articles.title: Woman Unknown review – postwar paranoia with some deliciously dastardly Du Maurier touches
articles.summary: Venice film festival A nanny becomes the new lady of a prosperous Copenhagen house as accused Nazi sympathisers are violently shamed in May el-Toukhy’s shrewd, painful portrait of survival.
body: Here is an elegantly appointed drama-thriller from May el-Toukhy, about sexual shame and political paranoia in postwar Denmark, with something of Alfred Hitchcock’s Rebecca, which it consciously recalls. As director and co-writer, El-Toukhy has created a shrewd and painful movie about the terrible things you need to do to survive, and what it takes to forget those things afterwards.

The scene is a prosperous, upper-middle-class apartment in Copenhagen just after the second world war, when the Danish resistance was permitted the powers of a secret-police militia to detain and interrogate those suspected of having given assistance to the Nazis. Christian (Carsten Bjørnlund) is a ageing factory owner and widower who has evidently fallen in love with his infant daughter’s nanny: this is Marie (fiercely and convincingly played by Mathilde Arcel). Or at any rate, he sees that the child needs a new mother, finds Marie attractive and appreciates her submissive attitude. They are now engaged.

articles.title: ‘The Inbetweeners 3’ Movie Is a Go at Netflix With Original Lead Cast
articles.summary: Simon Bird, James Buckley, Blake Harrison and Joe Thomas will reprise their roles in the new film from creators Damon Beesley and Iain Morris, starting production on Monday.
body: If you’ve never loved anything before, apart from a car or a sandwich or The Inbetweeners, this news is for you! Netflix unveiled on Monday that a third movie in the raunchy franchise is moving ahead, with production beginning on Monday in the U.K. on The Inbetweeners 3, which the streamer described as “a continuation of the hugely popular sitcom and its two record-breaking films.”

The film is produced by Claire Jones alongside Banijay’s Patrick Holland and Fudge Park Production’s Mark Lesbirel. Caroline Levy, Caroline Leddy, Phil Gilbert, Suzanne Knight, Tom Jordan, Farhana Bhula for Film4, Morris and Beesley serve as executive producers.
“It’s been super-fun hanging out with our friends again, and we’re going to work hard every week to ensure there are no problemos making this new film for humans,” said Beesley and Morris.

The coming-of-age sitcom was originally broadcast on Channel 4 between 2008 and 2010, following the misadventures of suburban teenager Will McKenzie and his friends Simon Cooper, Neil Sutherland and Jay Cartwright at the fictional Rudge Park Comprehensive as they navigated school life, friendship and failed sexual encounters.

articles.title: ‘Ground Floor’ Is a Political Parable Full of Apathy, Absurdity – and Mold (Exclusive Clip and Chat)
articles.summary: Hungary's Gábor Reisz, winner of the 2023 best film award in Venice's Horizons section for 'Explanation for Everything,' returns to the Lido in the Venice Spotlight program with a quixotic tale and dark humor.
body: Franz Kafka and Don Quixote would feel right at home watching Ground Floor ( Földszint ), the new film from Hungarian auteur Gábor Reisz. But former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán would very likely not be amused.

The film, world-premiering at Venice on Thursday, Sept. 10, stars Ádám Tompa ( Blue Heron ) as Kristóf, a failed artist who, on a single day on which he and his wife want to go on a lake holiday, learns that he will become a father and discovers strange black mold in their apartment. To the exasperation of his wife, the usually apathetic man is spurred into rare action to solve the mold issue. He doesn’t even really know the people in the building. Can he fix the mold emergency and change things for the better?

articles.title: Andrew Scott feels the Pressure as 'unsung hero' in WW2 thriller
articles.summary: The actor reveals how he approached playing James Stagg, the "chilly" meteorologist key to D-Day's success.
body: Andrew Scott says he loved the challenge of his latest acting role in the film Pressure, as the meteorologist key to the success of World War Two's D-Day - the largest seaborne invasion in history.

“Group Captain James Stagg may not have been the most charming person, but I think he had a huge amount of humility in the face of nature. And that's one of the themes I think of the film," Scott tells the BBC.
"He appeared to me to be an extraordinarily interesting cinematic character, as well as an unsung hero from history."
Stagg played a crucial advisory role when US General Dwight D Eisenhower invaded Normandy, laying the foundations for the Allied victory in World War Two.
